short: Mass ratio = molar masses: H2:Cl2 = 2:71 = 1:35.5.
long: In H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl, the reactants combine mole-for-mole (1:1), so the mass ratio equals the molar-mass ratio: H2 (2 g/mol) to Cl2 (71 g/mol) = 2:71, which simplifies to 1:35.5.
trick: For a 1:1 mole-ratio reaction, the mass ratio of reactants is just their molar-mass ratio directly — no stoichiometric coefficients to juggle.

options.a: Correct — 2:71 simplifies to 1:35.5.
options.b: Wrong — doesn't simplify the ratio consistently.
options.c: Wrong — this doubles the chlorine side incorrectly.
options.d: Wrong — close to the right magnitude but not the exact simplified ratio.

long:
Relative atomic mass is the abundance-weighted average of isotope masses: 20×0.9092 + 21×0.0026 + 22×0.0882 = 18.184 + 0.0546 + 1.9404 = 20.179 ≈ 20.18 — matching neon's well-known real atomic mass.

**Note:** the source data marked 20.28 (option B) as correct — that doesn't match this calculation. The corrected answer, 20.18 (option A), is confirmed by both the arithmetic and the real, independently known atomic mass of neon.
trick: Weighted average = Σ(mass number × fractional abundance). Convert percentages to decimals before multiplying.

options.a: Correct — matches both the calculation and neon's real atomic mass (20.18).
options.b: Wrong — doesn't match the weighted-average calculation.
options.c: Wrong — too low given ²⁰Ne's dominant 90.92% share only gets you to 18.184 before adding the other isotopes.
options.d: Wrong — close, but not the precise weighted result.

short: Na+ coordination number in NaCl is 6 (rock-salt/octahedral structure).
long: NaCl crystallizes in the rock-salt structure, where each Na+ ion is surrounded by 6 Cl− ions (and vice versa) in an octahedral arrangement.
trick: NaCl-type (rock salt) structure = coordination number 6 for both ions — a very frequently tested crystal-structure fact.

options.b: Wrong — too low for the rock-salt structure.
options.c: Wrong — 4 is the coordination number for tetrahedral structures like zinc blende (ZnS), not NaCl.
options.d: Wrong — 8 is the coordination number for CsCl-type (body-centered) structures, not NaCl.

short: CO2 shows the greatest non-ideal behaviour among H2, He, N2, CO2 at 0°C.
long: Non-ideal (real-gas) behaviour increases with molecular size and intermolecular attractive forces. CO2 is larger and more polarizable than H2, He, or N2, giving it the strongest intermolecular forces and hence the greatest deviation from ideal-gas behaviour, especially near its boiling point.
trick: Smaller, lighter, weakly-interacting gases (H2, He) behave most ideally; larger, more polarizable, easily liquefiable gases (CO2) deviate most.

options.a: Wrong — helium is one of the most ideal gases known.
options.b: Correct — CO2 deviates most from ideal behaviour.
options.c: Wrong — hydrogen is also very close to ideal.
options.d: Wrong — nitrogen is fairly close to ideal too, less non-ideal than CO2.

short: By the (n+l) rule: 3p<4s<3d<5s in energy, so decreasing order is 5s>3d>4s>3p.
long: Using the Aufbau (n+l) rule: 3p has n+l=4, 4s has n+l=4 (lower n wins tie, so 3p<4s); 3d has n+l=5, 5s has n+l=5 (lower n wins, so 3d<5s). Combining: 3p < 4s < 3d < 5s in energy. Written from highest to lowest: 5s > 3d > 4s > 3p.
trick: For subshells with the same (n+l) value, the one with the smaller n has lower energy — this is the tie-breaker rule that separates 3p/4s and 3d/5s.

options.a: Wrong — puts 3p last, but 3p is actually the lowest-energy of the four.
options.b: Correct — 5s > 3d > 4s > 3p matches the (n+l) rule.
options.c: Wrong — 3p should be lowest, not highest.
options.d: Wrong — same issue, plus 5s/4s order is also swapped.

short: Cl⁻ has the [Ar] configuration — 8 electrons in its outermost (3rd) shell.
long: A chloride ion has gained one electron: 17+1 = 18 electrons total, giving the configuration 2, 8, 8 — an argon-like noble-gas configuration with 8 electrons in the outermost (n=3) shell.
trick: Cl⁻, like every ion that has 'completed the octet', ends up isoelectronic with the nearest noble gas — here, argon (18 electrons, 8 in the outer shell).

options.a: Wrong — 17 is chlorine's atomic number/total protons, not its outer-shell electron count.
options.b: Wrong — doesn't match the octet structure of Cl⁻.
options.c: Wrong — same.
options.d: Correct — 8 electrons complete the outer shell, matching argon's configuration.

short: VSEPR repulsion strength order: LP–LP > LP–BP > BP–BP.
long: In VSEPR theory, lone pairs occupy more space and repel more strongly than bonding pairs. The repulsion strength ranks: lone pair–lone pair (strongest) > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair (weakest).
trick: Lone pairs are 'fatter' (less constrained by a second nucleus), so any repulsion involving a lone pair is stronger than a repulsion between two bond pairs — LP-LP tops the list every time.

options.a: Correct — LP-LP > LP-BP > BP-BP is the standard VSEPR order.
options.b: Wrong — puts LP-BP ahead of LP-LP, which is backwards.
options.c: Wrong — puts BP-BP first, the weakest type of repulsion.
options.d: Wrong — same issue, BP-BP shouldn't be in the middle either.

short: In ice, each O atom is hydrogen-bonded to 4 H atoms (tetrahedral arrangement).
long: In the ice crystal lattice, each water molecule's oxygen forms 2 covalent O–H bonds within its own molecule and 2 additional hydrogen bonds to neighbouring water molecules' H atoms, giving each O atom a total of 4 H-atom connections arranged tetrahedrally.
trick: Ice's open, tetrahedral hydrogen-bonded network (each O linked to 4 H) is exactly why ice is less dense than liquid water — a classic paired fact worth remembering together.

options.a: Correct — 2 covalent + 2 hydrogen bonds = 4 H atoms per O.
options.b: Wrong — undercounts by one.
options.c: Wrong — only counts one covalent bond.
options.d: Wrong — only counts the 2 covalent bonds, ignoring the hydrogen bonds to neighbours.

short: ΔHf° for CO2(g) is about −394 kJ/mol (commonly cited as −393.5 kJ/mol).
long: The standard enthalpy of formation of carbon dioxide gas from its elements (C(graphite) + O2(g) → CO2(g)) is a well-established thermochemical value, approximately −393.5 kJ/mol, commonly rounded to −394 kJ/mol.
trick: CO2's formation is exothermic (heat released), so ΔHf° must be negative — that alone eliminates the +394 option immediately.

options.a: Correct — approximately −394 kJ/mol, the standard textbook value.
options.b: Wrong — wrong sign; formation of CO2 releases heat, it doesn't absorb it.
options.c: Wrong — magnitude off from the accepted value.
options.d: Wrong — close, but not the standard cited value.

short: In exothermic reactions, reactants have higher energy than products (excess energy is released as heat).
long: An exothermic reaction releases energy to the surroundings because the products end up at a lower energy state than the reactants — the energy difference is given off as heat.
trick: Exo = 'exit' (energy exits the system) → reactants start higher, products end lower. Endo = energy enters the system → reactants start lower, products end higher.

options.a: Correct — exothermic reactions have higher-energy reactants than products.
options.b: Wrong — endothermic reactions have the opposite: products higher than reactants.
options.c: Wrong — photochemical reactions aren't defined by this energy comparison specifically.
options.d: Wrong — non-spontaneous reactions aren't defined by this either.

trick: Glucose's molar mass (180 g/mol) combined with water's Kb (0.52°C/m) is one of the most commonly recycled colligative-properties setups — memorizing both numbers makes this instant.

short: Molal freezing point depression constant (Kf) of water is 1.86 °C/m.
long: Kf, the molal freezing point depression constant for water, is a fixed physical property equal to 1.86 °C per mole of solute per kg of solvent.
trick: Water's two colligative constants are both worth memorizing together: Kb = 0.52 °C/m (boiling), Kf = 1.86 °C/m (freezing) — freezing point depression is always the larger effect of the two.

options.b: Wrong — not water's Kf value.
options.c: Wrong — far too large.
options.d: Wrong — 0.52 is actually water's Kb (boiling point elevation constant), not Kf.

short: In a Zn-Cu galvanic cell, electrons flow externally from zinc (anode) to copper (cathode).
long: Zinc is the more reactive metal and acts as the anode, where it's oxidized (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻), releasing electrons into the external circuit. These electrons travel through the wire to the copper cathode, where reduction occurs (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu).
trick: Electrons always flow externally from anode to cathode (oxidation site to reduction site) in a galvanic cell — memorize 'An Ox, Red Cat' (Anode=Oxidation, Cathode=Reduction) to keep this straight.

options.c: Wrong — the porous partition/salt bridge carries ions internally, not electrons.
options.d: Correct — zinc (anode, oxidized) to copper (cathode, reduced).

short: Arrhenius equation gives a straight line of log K vs 1/T with a negative slope.
long: Taking the log of the Arrhenius equation (k = Ae^(−Ea/RT)) gives log k = log A − (Ea/2.303R)(1/T) — a straight line when plotting log k against 1/T, with a negative slope of −Ea/(2.303R). As 1/T increases (temperature decreases), log k decreases.
trick: This linearized Arrhenius plot is used experimentally to find activation energy Ea directly from the slope — always expect a straight line with negative slope, never a curve.

options.a: See diagram — doesn't match the expected straight-line, negative-slope shape.
options.b: Correct — the straight line with negative slope matching the linearized Arrhenius equation.
options.c: See diagram — doesn't match the expected shape.
options.d: See diagram — doesn't match the expected shape.

short: 2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl is the only complete, balanced redox reaction among the choices.
long: A redox reaction needs both oxidation and reduction happening together in one balanced equation. 2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl shows Na (0 → +1, oxidized) and Cl (0 → −1, reduced) simultaneously. The other options are either a non-redox double displacement (NaCl+AgNO3) or incomplete half-reactions (missing their other half).
trick: A genuine complete redox reaction must show a species being oxidized AND a species being reduced within the same balanced equation — a lone half-reaction with 'e⁻' floating on one side isn't a complete reaction.

options.a: Wrong — this is a double displacement/precipitation reaction; no oxidation states change.
options.b: Wrong — this is only the oxidation half-reaction, incomplete on its own.
options.c: Correct — shows both oxidation (Na) and reduction (Cl) in one complete equation.
options.d: Wrong — this is only the reduction half-reaction, incomplete on its own.

short: A substance that releases H+ in water is, by definition, an acid.
long: By the Arrhenius definition, an acid is a substance that dissociates in water to release hydrogen ions (H+).
trick: Arrhenius acid = releases H+ in water; Arrhenius base = releases OH− in water. This is the most basic acid-base definition and usually the one intended unless a question specifies Bronsted-Lowry or Lewis theory.

options.a: Correct — this is the Arrhenius definition of an acid.
options.b: Wrong — bases release OH−, not H+.
options.c: Wrong — amphoteric substances can act as both, not defined by releasing only H+.
options.d: Wrong — neutral substances don't release H+ or OH− in a way that shifts pH from 7.

short: Normal blood pH is tightly maintained around 7.35–7.4 (physiological range ~7.35–7.45).
long: Human blood pH is buffered (mainly by the bicarbonate buffer system) to stay within a narrow physiological range, typically cited as 7.35–7.45, closely matching the 7.35–7.4 option given here.
trick: Blood pH is very slightly basic (above 7), not neutral or acidic — even a small deviation outside 7.35–7.45 is medically dangerous (acidosis/alkalosis).

options.a: Wrong — too wide/high a range for blood pH.
options.b: Wrong — too high for normal blood.
options.c: Wrong — slightly too high.
options.d: Correct — matches the physiological blood pH range.

short: Zero order reaction: rate is independent of reactant concentration.
long: For a zero-order reaction, rate = k[A]⁰ = k — a constant, unaffected by changes in reactant concentration.
trick: Reaction order tells you how sensitive the rate is to concentration: zero order = no dependence at all, first order = directly proportional, second order = proportional to the square.

options.a: Wrong — the definition concerns reactant concentration, not product.
options.b: Correct — rate is unaffected by reactant concentration in a zero-order reaction.
options.c: Wrong — rate constant k itself still depends on temperature (via Arrhenius); it's concentration that's independent, not temperature.
options.d: Wrong — surface area relates to heterogeneous catalysis, not the definition of reaction order.

short: Across a period, melting/boiling points first rise (to a mid-period peak) then fall sharply.
long: Moving across a period, melting/boiling points generally rise as metallic/covalent network bonding strengthens (peaking around Group 14, e.g. carbon or silicon), then fall sharply for the molecular non-metals and drop to a minimum for the noble gases.
trick: Picture Period 3: Na, Mg, Al rise steadily (metallic bonding strengthens); Si peaks (giant covalent network); then P, S, Cl, Ar drop off fast (small, separate molecules with only weak van der Waals forces).

options.a: Wrong — the trend doesn't dip first.
options.b: Wrong — it doesn't rise the whole way across; it drops sharply after the peak.
options.c: Correct — rises to a mid-period peak, then decreases.

short: Atomic radius shrinks across a period due to increasing nuclear charge (more protons), not more shells.
long:
Across a period, the number of electron shells stays exactly the same — that's the definition of a period. What changes is the number of protons in the nucleus, increasing the effective nuclear charge, which pulls the same-shell electrons in more tightly, shrinking the atomic radius.

**Note:** the source data marked 'increase in number of shells' as correct — this is inconsistent with the very definition of a period, since shell count only increases *down* a group, never across a period. The corrected answer is the increasing nuclear charge (more protons), which is the actual textbook explanation for this trend.
trick: Shells increase down a group (radius increases); nuclear charge increases across a period (radius decreases). Don't mix up which trend belongs to which direction.

options.a: Wrong — more valence electrons alone doesn't explain the radius decrease; it's the increased pull from the nucleus that does.
options.b: Correct — more protons increase nuclear charge, pulling electrons in tighter.
options.c: Wrong — shell count doesn't decrease across a period at all.
options.d: Wrong — shell count stays constant across a period; it doesn't increase (that only happens down a group).

short: MgO is the least soluble alkaline earth oxide in water (solubility increases down the group).
long: Solubility of Group 2 (alkaline earth) metal oxides in water increases going down the group (Mg → Ca → Sr → Ba). Being at the top of the group, MgO is the least soluble of the four listed.
trick: Down a group, ionic lattice energy decreases faster than hydration energy for these oxides, favouring dissolution — so solubility trends increase going down Group 2, the opposite of some other Group 2 property trends.

options.a: Correct — MgO, at the top of the group, is the least soluble.
options.b: Wrong — CaO is more soluble than MgO.
options.c: Wrong — BaO, at the bottom of the group, is the most soluble of the four.
options.d: Wrong — SrO is more soluble than MgO.

long: Carbon monoxide is represented with a triple bond between carbon and oxygen (:C≡O:), giving both atoms a formal octet, with a lone pair on each atom, matching the diagram's structure A.
trick: CO is isoelectronic with N2, and just like N2's strong triple bond, CO also has a triple bond — one of the strongest bonds known in a diatomic molecule.

short: FeSO4 and FeCl2 both have Fe²⁺ (same oxidation state).
long: Checking each pair: FeSO4 has Fe²⁺ (sulfate is −2), FeCl3 has Fe³⁺ (three chlorides, each −1) — different states. FeCl2 has Fe²⁺ (two chlorides). So FeSO4 and FeCl2 both have Fe²⁺ — matching oxidation states.
trick: Work out Fe's oxidation state from the known charge of the counter-ion/anion in each compound: sulfate is always −2, chloride is always −1 per ion.

short: K3[Fe(CN)6] is potassium ferricyanide — Fe is +3.
long:
Three K+ ions contribute +3 total charge, balanced against the complex anion [Fe(CN)6]³⁻. Six CN⁻ ligands contribute −6. So Fe's oxidation state + (−6) = −3, giving Fe = +3. This compound is named potassium ferricyanide precisely because of the +3 ('ferri-') iron — contrast with K4[Fe(CN)6], potassium ferrocyanide, where Fe is +2 ('ferro-').

**Note:** the source data marked +2 as correct — that's the oxidation state for the *ferrocyanide* ion K4[Fe(CN)6] (four potassiums, not three). Since this formula explicitly has three K+, the corrected answer is +3.
trick: Count the potassium ions: K3[Fe(CN)6] (3 K, ferri-, Fe³⁺) vs K4[Fe(CN)6] (4 K, ferro-, Fe²⁺) — a classic paired fact worth memorizing together to avoid mixing them up.

options.b: Correct — balancing charges with 3 K+ and 6 CN⁻ gives Fe³⁺.
options.c: Wrong — oxidation states of metals in these complexes aren't negative.
options.d: Wrong — same reasoning as C.

short: Conventionally, aqueous ammonia is classified as a weak base.
long:
NH3 dissolved in water reacts as NH3 + H2O ⇌ NH4+ + OH−, making it a classic weak base (this is the textbook NH4OH example paired with acetic acid as the standard weak acid/weak base pair).

**Note:** the source data marks this as 'Amphoteric' — under a strict Bronsted-Lowry view, ammonia can in principle act as a very weak acid too (losing H+ to form NH2−), but this only happens under extreme, non-aqueous conditions (e.g. self-ionization of liquid ammonia). In ordinary aqueous chemistry — which is what this question describes — ammonia's behaviour is overwhelmingly basic, not amphoteric in the practical sense (unlike Al(OH)3 or ZnO, which readily react with both acids and bases in water). Left as the source's chosen answer, but this classification is unusual against the standard convention.
trick: Substances genuinely called 'amphoteric' in the aqueous-chemistry sense (Al2O3, ZnO, Al(OH)3, water itself) react readily with BOTH acids and bases under normal conditions — aqueous NH3 does not react with bases, so calling it amphoteric is non-standard.

options.b: This is the conventional classification, though not the source's marked answer.
options.c: Wrong — ammonia doesn't behave as an acid in ordinary aqueous chemistry.
options.d: Wrong — pure water is neutral, but dissolved ammonia clearly shifts the solution's pH above 7.

short: Unpolluted rainwater has a pH of about 5.6, due to dissolved atmospheric CO2 forming weak carbonic acid.
long: Even without pollution, rainwater is naturally slightly acidic because atmospheric CO2 dissolves into it, forming carbonic acid (CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3), giving a natural equilibrium pH around 5.6 — distinct from 'acid rain', which is far more acidic due to sulfur/nitrogen oxide pollutants.
trick: 5.6 is the benchmark for *natural* unpolluted rain; genuine acid rain drops well below this (often pH 4 or lower) due to added SO2/NOx pollution.

short: N2's strong triple bond makes it very unreactive, though not completely inert like the noble gases.
long: Nitrogen's N≡N triple bond has very high bond energy (~945 kJ/mol), making N2 kinetically very unreactive under ordinary conditions. However, it isn't truly inert — it does react under specific conditions (Haber process, lightning-driven NO formation, biological nitrogen fixation), unlike noble gases which essentially never react.
trick: 'Very unreactive' ≠ 'completely inert' — N2 needs a real push (high pressure/temperature/catalyst, lightning, or specialized enzymes) to react, but it can be made to react, unlike true noble gases.

long: The industrial synthesis of ammonia (N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3) uses an iron catalyst, typically enhanced with small amounts of metal oxide promoters (like Al2O3 and K2O) to improve its efficiency and lifespan.
trick: Haber process = Iron catalyst (with promoters) — a fixed, well-known industrial chemistry fact worth memorizing directly.

trick: Cis = 'same side' (like groups together); Trans = 'across' (like groups on opposite sides) — a quick way to identify which structure is which in a diagram.

NO2+ (nitronium ion) is electron-poor (an electrophile), and N+H4 (ammonium) has no available lone pair since all four bonding positions on nitrogen are already used.
trick: Look for a lone pair AND either a neutral or negative charge — species with a '+' and no free lone pair (like NH4+) can't act as nucleophiles.

long: Friedel-Crafts alkylation introduces an alkyl group onto benzene using an alkyl halide (R-X, here R-Cl) activated by a Lewis acid catalyst like AlCl3, which generates a carbocation electrophile (R+) that attacks the benzene ring.
trick: Alkylation uses R-Cl (alkyl halide) + AlCl3; Acylation (making a ketone instead) uses R-COCl (acyl chloride) + AlCl3 — don't mix up these two closely related Friedel-Crafts reactions.

long: Propene (CH3-CH=CH2) reacting with HBr (no peroxides) follows Markovnikov's rule: H adds to the carbon that already has more hydrogens (the terminal CH2), and Br adds to the more substituted carbon, giving 2-bromopropane (CH3-CHBr-CH3) as the major product — matching the diagram's structure D.
trick: Markovnikov's rule: 'the rich get richer' — H goes to the carbon already holding more H atoms, and the halogen ends up on the more substituted carbon.

long: Reactivity in nucleophilic substitution correlates with how weak the carbon-halogen bond is (and how good a leaving group the halide is). C-I is the weakest bond (largest, most polarizable I), making RI most reactive; C-F is the strongest bond, making RF least reactive.
trick: Bond strength order C-F > C-Cl > C-Br > C-I is the reverse of reactivity order RI > RBr > RCl > RF — weaker bond, better leaving group, faster substitution.

trick: Aqueous KOH favours substitution (OH⁻ is a strong nucleophile in water); alcoholic KOH favours elimination (the alkoxide base pulls off a proton instead of attacking carbon) — this solvent choice is a frequently tested distinction.

long:
This is the standard test reaction for detecting an -OH group: an alcohol reacting with PCl5 produces the alkyl chloride, phosphorus oxychloride (POCl3), and HCl gas (observed as white, misty fumes) — all three products together.

**Note:** the source data marked the answer as just 'C2H5Cl and HCl', omitting POCl3 — but the complete, balanced reaction always produces all three products. The corrected answer includes POCl3.

long: 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, commonly known as picric acid, is a phenol ring bearing an OH group and three nitro (NO2) substituents at the 2, 4, and 6 positions.

short: The methyl ketone group (CH3-CO-R) gives a positive iodoform test.
long: The iodoform test (yellow CHI3 precipitate) is positive for compounds containing a methyl ketone group (CH3-CO-R) or a CH3-CH(OH)- group, since the alkaline iodine first oxidizes/halogenates the methyl group attached to the carbonyl and cleaves it off as iodoform.

short: Phenol + bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol, a white precipitate.
long: Phenol's activated ring (from the OH group's electron donation) undergoes rapid electrophilic bromination at the 2, 4, and 6 positions even with just bromine water (no catalyst needed), forming 2,4,6-tribromophenol, which precipitates as a white solid.
trick: Phenol reacting instantly with bromine water (no catalyst!) to decolorize it and form a white precipitate is a classic qualitative test for phenols — contrast with benzene, which needs a Lewis acid catalyst to brominate at all.

short: Increasing acid strength: Water < Ethanol < Phenol < Carboxylic acid.
long: Carboxylic acids are strongest (resonance-stabilized conjugate base). Phenol is next (its conjugate base, phenoxide, is also resonance-stabilized, though less so). Water is next — slightly more acidic than ethanol because ethanol's electron-donating ethyl group destabilizes its conjugate base (ethoxide) more than water's conjugate base (hydroxide) is destabilized. Ethanol is the weakest acid of the four.
trick: It's counterintuitive, but water is slightly MORE acidic than ethanol — the alkyl group's electron-donating (+I) effect in ethanol makes its conjugate base less stable, so ethanol holds onto its proton slightly more tightly than water does.

options.d: Wrong — this reverses the entire order (would describe increasing strength left to right, but water isn't the strongest acid here).

short: 1-phenylethanol (a secondary alcohol) oxidizes to acetophenone.

trick: Secondary alcohols oxidize to ketones; primary alcohols oxidize to aldehydes (then carboxylic acids); tertiary alcohols resist oxidation entirely — always check which class of alcohol is needed to get the target product.

short: Fischer esterification is a nucleophilic (acyl) substitution reaction.
long: In acid-catalyzed ester formation, the alcohol's oxygen (nucleophile) attacks the protonated carboxylic acid's electrophilic carbonyl carbon, ultimately substituting -OH with -OR' — classified as nucleophilic (acyl) substitution.
trick: Ester formation from a carboxylic acid + alcohol always falls under nucleophilic acyl substitution — the alcohol is the nucleophile attacking the carbonyl carbon.

short: CH3-CN (methyl cyanide) hydrolyzes to CH3-COOH — acetic acid, not formic acid.
long:
Nitrile hydrolysis (R-CN + 2H2O + H+/OH− → R-COOH + NH3) adds a carbon-bearing carboxyl group onto the R group already present. Methyl cyanide is CH3-CN, so hydrolysis gives CH3-COOH — acetic acid (2 carbons total).

**Note:** the source data marked formic acid (HCOOH, 1 carbon) as correct — but formic acid would only result from hydrolyzing HCN, not CH3CN. Since the carbon count must be preserved (CH3-CN has 2 carbons: the methyl carbon plus the nitrile carbon, both ending up in CH3-COOH), the corrected answer is acetic acid.
trick: Nitrile hydrolysis keeps the same number of carbons as the starting nitrile — R-CN → R-COOH, no carbons lost or gained.

long: Standard biological (alpha) amino acids have both an amino and a carboxyl group on the same central (alpha) carbon. In solution near neutral pH, the amino group is protonated (NH3+) and the carboxyl group is deprotonated (COO−) simultaneously, giving a net-neutral but internally charged 'zwitterion' — this dipolar form dominates for alpha amino acids specifically.
